title: E2E response timeline sampler - observations and playbacks
body:
Purpose
This note captures a focused sampling run and early forensic observations from a week-long e2e trace capture across canary traffic for model: rwinf-7b-infer-v2. Goal: understand the dominant contributors to p95/p99 latency inflations we saw on 2025-11-03 and to suggest quick mitigations we can A/B. This is an informal working doc — rough reproductions, hypotheses, and short playbook items.

Instrumentation and sampling method
- Collection window: 2025-11-03 00:00 -> 2025-11-09 23:59 UTC.
- Traffic subset: 3% canary traffic routed to canary pool with instrumented tracing.
- Traces collected via x-trace-id propagated across front proxy -> router -> runtime -> gpu-worker -> postproc. Each span includes: start_ts, end_ts, stage_name, seq_len, model_variant, batch_size, kv_hit (true/false), cold_start (true/false), queue_depth_at_enqueue, host_zone.
- Sampling: head-based sampler that kept every trace with total latency > 350ms plus uniform 0.05% baseline sample for distribution calibration.
- Aggregation: per-stage duration computed as end_ts - start_ts; end-to-end is sum of stage durations plus small network egress jitter recorded separately.

Quick numbers (aggregated from 12k retained traces)
- Overall E2E (all seq_lens): p50 = 122ms, p95 = 342ms, p99 = 790ms.
- Cold-KV subset (first request to model session, kv_hit=false): p50 = 205ms, p95 = 620ms, p99 = 1,450ms.
- Hot-KV subset (kv_hit=true): p50 = 110ms, p95 = 210ms, p99 = 360ms.

Per-stage median and tail (representative):
(Ordered as happened in trace)
- Front proxy (ingress LB): p50=6ms p95=18ms p99=40ms
- Request decode & auth: p50=1ms p95=5ms p99=10ms
- Router dispatch: p50=4ms p95=12ms p99=28ms (note: includes cross-service RPCs for model pin resolution)
- KV lookup (prefix cache read): p50=2ms p95=120ms p99=520ms (bimodal; see notes)
- Worker queue wait (pre-GPU enqueue): p50=8ms p95=62ms p99=380ms
- GPU forward (model compute): p50=70ms p95=85ms p99=110ms (scales with seq_len)
- KV write (post-forward update): p50=3ms p95=18ms p99=60ms
- Postprocessing/serialization: p50=18ms p95=25ms p99=40ms
- Egress/transport jitter: median 10ms, tail 30–80ms depending on dst region

Key observations (what stands out)
1) KV lookup bimodality drives the high tail:
   - The KV lookup stage shows a strong bimodal distribution. Most requests hit a fast in-memory lookup (p50 ~2ms), but ~2.8% of traces hit remote-cache fallback or disk-backed TTL rehydration, producing 100ms–500ms delays. Those traces align almost perfectly with p99 spikes overall.
   - Root causes guessed: per-host cache evictions on hot rotation windows + occasional network hiccups to remote cache tier.
2) Queue wait amplifies burstiness at p99:
   - Worker queue wait correlates with p99 events where queue_depth_at_enqueue spikes > 60. Many of these traces share a common hour window with sudden burst of long-seq requests (>1.5x average seq_len).
   - The runtime's continuous batching knob max_batch_wait_ms=12ms currently allows larger batches to form under bursty input; that reduces cost for p50 but increases p99 due to head-of-line waiting.
3) Cold-KV traces dominate the extreme tail:
   - When kv_hit=false and a rehydrate was required, p99 > 1.4s is common: sequence is remote fetch (150–400ms), slot into GPU queue (additional 200–500ms), then model compute.
4) GPU compute is not the main culprit for tail beyond seq_len scaling:
   - Per-worker GPU forward is fairly tight; even for longer sequences the compute variance doesn't eclipse the queue and KV delays. This implies optimization levers should prioritize cache stability and batching policy.
5) Cross-service routing occasionally adds 10–30ms (seen at p95) when metadata resolution falls back to control plane in the same request; those are fixable by simple caching of pin metadata on router for 1–2s windows.

Trace archetypes (handful)
- Fast path (majority, ~86%): front proxy (8ms) -> router (6ms) -> kv(hit) (2ms) -> worker queue (6ms) -> gpu (70ms) -> postproc (18ms) = ~110–140ms total.
- KV-fallback path (~9%): kv miss -> remote fetch (200ms) -> queue wait (40–120ms) -> gpu -> postproc = 380–720ms.
- Burst-head path (~2.5%): many long-seq requests arrive concurrently -> queue wait spikes (>200ms) while batch grows -> gpu -> postproc = 600–1450ms (when combined with KV fallback you get >1s).

Reproduction notes
- Synthetic playback that recreates the p99 shape: replay 1200 requests over 10s with a mix: 10% long seq (2.5x median), 5% cold sessions (kv_hit=false). Playback against canary pool with production-like routing reproduces p95~350ms and p99~790ms.
- When we capped max_batch_wait_ms to 4ms in a small experiment, p50 increased slightly (~+8ms) but p99 dropped ~22%.

Immediate mitigation candidates (fast experiments)
- Short-term (1–2 days):
  * Reduce max_batch_wait_ms from 12ms -> 6ms for canary pool A/B; observe p50/p95/p99 tradeoff. (low risk config flip)
  * Add 1s in-router metadata cache for model_pin resolution to eliminate intermittent router 10–30ms tails.
  * Increase KV in-memory reservation for hot-key set (temporary policy): bump LRU threshold for 10s windows to avoid eviction storms during rotation windows.
- Medium-term (1–3 weeks):
  * Introduce fast-path scheduling for small batches and small seq_len: an expedited queue with bounded capacity so tiny requests do not get stuck behind large-batch assembly.
  * Improve remote-kv fallback: parallelize remote fetch with initial enqueue to GPU queue where possible (specifically allow overlapping remote-kv + early GPU enqueue for cache-rehydra tolerant cases).
  * Autoscaler tuning: add spike-detection rule to spin up workers when queue_depth gradient > threshold within 30s.

Longer-term ideas (design tickets)
- Per-model adaptive batching policy: use running distribution of seq_len and kv-miss rate to set per-model max_batch_wait_ms and batch_size_target dynamically.
- Hierarchical KV: keep a tiny per-worker hot cache (1–2k entries) for absolute hottest prefixes plus the existing shared cache. Reduces remote fetch proportion for the top percentile.
- Trace-driven SLA alerts: auto-generate p95/p99 regressions per-stage and open a linear ticket with attached representative traces when stage contribution to p99 increases > 2x baseline.

Action items (owner -> task)
- Ava Chen (owner): run A/B with max_batch_wait_ms=6ms on canary, collect 48h traces; compare p50/p95/p99 (due 2026-01-19).
- Diego Morales: prototype short-lived router metadata cache (PR linked) and run canary rollout (due 2026-01-16).
- Priya Natarajan: produce a kv-eviction heatmap for the last 7 days and identify top-1k prefixes by churn (due 2026-01-20).
- Liam O'Connor: implement fast-path queue prototype for small-batch scheduling (spike experiment; due 2026-02-02).

Open questions / unknowns
- Is remote cache network hiccup correlated with specific host_zone or external infra events? Need SRE correlation.
- How often are model-pin control-plane fallbacks happening and why did router have misses during the window?
- Are there request patterns from a small set of tenants causing the long-seq bursts? Need request attribution.

Appendix: sample trace lines (CSV: trace_id, total_ms, seq_len, kv_hit, queue_wait_ms, gpu_ms, notes)

trc-0149,402,42,false,38,86,kv-rehydrate

Notes to reviewers
- This is iteration 0 for the playback-led forensics — expect follow-ups with more rigorous bucketed stats and per-tenant breakdowns.
- If you run the canary flips, please keep the full trace header retention policy for at least 72h; anonymize request payloads for privacy.

End of doc
